Estrogen Exposure Shields the Aging Brain
items.sum: Does lifetime estrogen protect the brain's microcirculation? A 5-year MRI study in Neurology reveals that a longer reproductive lifespan and hormone therapy use cut cerebral small vessel disease burden by up to 59%, preserving white matter integrity into older age.

The Acoustic Science of What Makes a Great Singer
items.sum: What separates a good opera singer from a great one in the ears of competition judges? Keio University researchers simulated a live vocal competition, revealing that the 2–4 kHz "singer’s formant" and sex-specific vibrato tuning drive top marks, while raw loudness matters little.

items.title: How Octopuses Lock in Long-Term Memory Without New Proteins
items.sum: How does an octopus hold onto memories without the molecular machinery used by humans? Researchers discovered a self-sustaining nitric oxide switch in the octopus vertical lobe that locks in long-term potentiation without requiring new protein synthesis.

items.title: 여성호르몬 에스트로겐, 치매 예방에도 도움될까…새 연구 주목 > 시애틀 뉴스/핫이슈
Enriched Environments Rewire the Brain via Shared Synaptic Gene Networks
items.sum: How does an active, stimulating lifestyle physically rewire the brain? A meta-analysis of over 300 studies identifies a conserved molecular signature driven by the AP-1 transcription factor, unveiling the genomic machinery behind environmental enrichment.

items.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
items.sum: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

Glioblastoma’s Chaos Follows Predictable Rules
items.sum: Is glioblastoma's deadly chaos actually predictable? Researchers analyzed over one million tumor cells to uncover the hidden rules governing brain cancer plasticity, using AI to identify molecular switches that reprogram malignant cells into harmless states.

items.title: One Autism Mutation Collapses the Whole Gene Network
items.sum: How can hundreds of different mutations cause autism? Boston Children's Hospital researchers discovered "transcriptomic convergence"—where mutating one autism gene drags down a whole network—and identified ZFX, an X-linked gene that protects females from the collapse.

Why Bitter Coffee Starts to Taste So Good to Your Brain
items.sum: Why do we learn to love the bitter taste of coffee? A study in Nature led by UCSF reveals an internal "slow" dopamine circuit connecting gut nutrient sensors to the left amygdala, building over minutes to link post-ingestive caloric rewards with new flavors.

Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
items.sum: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

The three-banded panther worm is rewriting the story of brain evolution
items.sum: The animal has a brain structure all its own, according to a 2026 preprint. The finding hints that brains could have evolved centralization before regionalization.

items.sum: Michael Cole explains how "brain flows" are the fundamental units of brain function and cognition.

Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
items.sum: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to gr

items.title: Omega-3 DHA Eases Autism Behaviors by Calming Inflammation
items.sum: Can omega-3 fatty acids reshape brain circuits in autism? A study in Pediatric Discovery demonstrates that DHA reduces repetitive behaviors and restores sociability in early-stress rat models by blocking the prefrontal JNK inflammatory cascade and boosting NRF2 antioxidant enzymes.

items.title: Neuromorphic Chip Decodes Brain’s Emotion Waves
items.sum: Can wearable brain monitors track emotions without draining batteries? Beijing Institute of Technology researchers developed a neuromorphic spiking neural network and asynchronous accelerator that decodes emotional states from EEG in 18 microseconds, using 97.5% less energy than conventional AI.

items.title: How Video Gamers Make Split-Second Decisions
items.sum: Can 5,000 hours of Counter-Strike sharpen your real-world reflexes? University of Sheffield researchers tested over 300 players, discovering a 90-millisecond mental processing edge in visual decision speed, but zero advantage in multitasking.

items.title: The Dark Side of Bonding With AI Companions
items.sum: Can a software update break a human heart? A study shows that while people find comfort in AI companions, they suffer acute anxiety and vulnerability fearing developers will alter or erase their digital partners.

items.title: Your voice can now say things you never said
items.sum: Synthetic voices can restore speech, enable scams and outlive their owners. These uses raise questions about trust, consent and control.

items.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.sum: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism

items.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.sum: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.title: 과식 조절하는 뇌 신경회로, 암수에서 달랐다…새로운 식욕 조절 경로 발견
‘Brain Flows: How Network Dynamics Compose the Human Mind,’ an excerpt
items.sum: In his new book, published today, Michael W. Cole examines how the movement of neuronal activity between neuronal populations shapes free will, intelligence and creativity. In this excerpt from Chapter 1, Cole explores why activity flows could unify efforts to map brain functions and connectivity.

items.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
items.sum: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
items.sum: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps

items.title: Menopause Blood Protein Signature Tied to Dementia Risk
items.sum: How does menopause shape long-term brain health? A new study of 12,000 women reveals that a panel of 16 blood proteins linked to brain aging surges during the menopause transition, offering a midlife window to screen for future dementia risk.

New Stanford initiative aims to build digital twin of human brain
items.sum: The effort, funded by private donors, seeks to train the model on a trove of MRI and magnetoencephalography data that scientists plan to collect over the next five years—but questions about its scientific utility and feasibility remain.

items.title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
items.sum: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.

The genome offers a recipe, not a blueprint, for the brain
items.sum: During brain development, genes set the rules and turn the knobs; self-organization does much of the rest.

items.title: Autism research involving monkeys contends with uphill battle
items.sum: Macaques and marmosets recapitulate the condition’s core traits better than mice can, but funding uncertainty and challenges at primate centers in the United States could make this work difficult to continue.

items.title: When is self-organization a mechanism in brain development?
items.sum: Retinal waves offer a powerful example of a self-organizing system that can build structure without external guidance. The field would do well to embrace such phenomena more broadly as a type of mechanistic explanation.

Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
items.sum: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
items.sum: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
items.sum: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzh

items.title: Fly taste connectome traces paths from sensation to action
items.sum: The map—the first of its kind for an animal more complex than Caenorhabditis elegans —gives neuroscientists a trove of testable hypotheses about how neuronal circuits guide feeding behaviors.

items.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
items.sum: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medic

items.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
items.sum: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

items.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
items.sum: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not es

items.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
items.sum: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.

items.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
items.sum: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people h

items.title: How brain implants turn thoughts into speech
items.sum: New brain-computer interfaces turn attempted speech into words and can speak them in a voice resembling the user’s own.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
items.sum: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively h

items.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
items.sum: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain

items.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
items.sum: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart

items.title: Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
items.sum: Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.

items.title: Why did humans’ brains surpass chimps’? A tiny foe might help explain it
items.sum: A viral infection from millions of years ago may have influenced chimp brain evolution through DNA leftovers in the genome.

items.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
items.sum: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
items.sum: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
items.sum: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

items.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
items.sum: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
items.sum: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.

items.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable
items.sum: The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

items.title: AI can give you your voice back
items.sum: People who have lost the ability to talk are finding new voices with technology. This technological feat is changing what it means to lose a voice.

items.title: Scientists find a way to fight Alzheimer’s brain damage without removing toxic tau
items.sum: Scientists have found a promising way to protect the brain from Alzheimer’s-related damage by blocking immune cells that contribute to the destruction of neurons. In mice, the treatment preserved roughly 40% more tissue in memory centers and improved memory, even without removing harmful tau protein buildup.

items.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
items.sum: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

items.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
items.sum: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. items.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
items.sum: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

items.title: Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
items.sum: The technology could get those with ALS, Parkinson’s disease and brain injuries “talking” again.

items.title: What happens when you lose your voice?
items.sum: Losing your voice can feel like losing part of yourself. Can voice-cloning technology help people find themselves again?

items.title: Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
items.sum: Scientists know APOE4 raises Alzheimer’s risk. A surprising change in blood vessel cells may help explain how.

items.title: Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science
items.sum: An icy window into the cosmos, a light switch for the brain and solving the mystery of mirror image molecules all took home the top prize.

items.title: Gene therapy and special goggles give some blind people limited sight
items.sum: Optogenetics, recognized by the 2026 medicine Nobel, makes cells respond to light, including eye cells that normally relay signals to the brain.

items.title: ‘A Mother’s Brain’ explores the neuroscience of motherhood
items.sum: Neuroscientist Susana Carmona’s book guides readers through a new mom’s changing brain.
